b: A. The epidemiological triad is a model used to understand the causation and spread of infectious diseases. It comprises three components :
Agent – The cause of the disease (e.g., bacteria, virus, parasite, toxin).
Host – The human or animal affected by the disease.
Environment – External factors that influence the agent and the host interaction (e.g., climate, sanitation, living conditions).
These three interact dynamically to result in disease occurrence. Interruption of any link can prevent disease. (6 marks)
Definition: Immunologically mediated inflammatory lung disease primarily affecting the alveoli (not bronchi like asthma)
Also called: Allergic Alveolitis
Most often an occupational disease from heightened sensitivity to inhaled antigens
Classic example: Farmer's Lung (moldy hay — thermophilic actinomycetes)
Manifests as predominantly restrictive lung disease with:
Group of conditions characterized by infiltration and activation of eosinophils in the lung
Elevated alveolar IL-5 drives eosinophil activation
Generally immunologic in origin; etiology often unknown
Many collagen vascular diseases have pulmonary manifestations:
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)
Dermatomyositis-polymyositis

es.q: What is the core mechanism of ENDOCRINE & RENAL PATHOLOGY — MUST KNOW NOTES? → Explain the key pathological or physiological process.
es.m:
- **Core Process:** Disruption of hormonal regulation or renal filtration mechanisms leading to systemic metabolic and electrolyte imbalances.
- **Endocrine Pathophysiology:** Involves hormone excess (e.g., cortisol in Cushing's, aldosterone in Conn's) or hormone deficiency (e.g., cortisol/aldosterone in Addison's disease, insulin in Type 1 diabetes).
- **Renal Pathophysiology:** Rapid or progressive decline in nephron function categorized into prerenal, intrinsic (such as acute tubular necrosis), or postrenal etiologies.

es.q: Which finding most strongly supports ENDOCRINE & RENAL PATHOLOGY — MUST KNOW NOTES clinically? → Identify the highest-yield clue.
es.m:
- **Hyperpigmentation:** Strongly supports primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) due to elevated ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone co-secretion.
- **Paroxysmal Hypertension TRIAD:** Episodic headaches, sweating, and tachycardia highly suggest phaeochromocytoma.
- **Electrolyte Derangements:** Hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia point specifically to primary mineralocorticoid deficiency.
- **Urine Output Drops:** Oliguria or anuria combined with a rising serum creatinine strongly points toward acute kidney injury (AKI).
- **Metabolic Acidosis with Kussmaul Breathing:** Highly indicative of acute diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in Type 1 diabetes.

ai.title: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Immunologically mediated inflammatory lung disease affecting the alveoli, often occupational. Presents with restrictive physiology and can progress to fibrosis if exposure continues.

sections.p: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) is an immune‑mediated inflammatory reaction of the alveoli and interstitium to inhaled organic antigens.
b: Diagnosis requires compatible exposure, clinical picture, and supportive investigations.
Acute HP: fever, cough, dyspnoea 4–8 h after exposure.
Sub‑acute/chronic HP: insidious dyspnoea, dry cough, weight loss.

sections.p: HP is staged by duration and radiologic pattern rather than a formal numeric score.
b: Acute: symptom onset within hours, normal or mildly abnormal chest X‑ray.
Sub‑acute: weeks to months, ground‑glass opacities on CT.
Chronic: >6 months, fibrosis, honey‑comb on CT, reduced DLCO.

sections.p: Common antigens in low‑resource African settings are listed by exposure type.
b: Moldy hay or stored grain (thermophilic actinomycetes) – farmer’s lung.
Bird droppings or feathers – pigeon‑breeder’s lung.
Moldy home‑grown maize or millet – “moldy corn” lung.
Dust from wood, saw‑dust, or herbal preparations.

sections.p: History of recent exposure is key; physical exam often shows inspiratory crackles and, in chronic disease, clubbing.
b: Fever, chills, malaise in acute phase.
Dry, non‑productive cough.
Progressive exertional dyspnoea.
Fine end‑inspiratory crackles; late clubbing.

t.b: Shows early diffuse haziness or later reticular pattern; if unavailable, proceed to clinical staging.
Detects ground‑glass opacities, centrilobular nodules, and fibrosis; if CT not available, use chest X‑ray plus spirometry.
Demonstrates restrictive defect (reduced FVC) and reduced diffusion capacity (DLCO); normal values do not exclude early disease.
Identify specific antigen sensitisation; negative test does not rule out HP.
Lymphocytosis (>20 %) supports diagnosis; unavailable in many settings – rely on clinical picture.
Shows interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate and poorly formed granulomas; not required if other criteria met.

sections.p: Failure to remove antigen can lead to irreversible fibrosis and respiratory failure.
b: Rapid progression of dyspnoea despite avoidance.
Development of pulmonary hypertension.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) after massive exposure.

sections.p: Mainstay is antigen avoidance; steroids are used for symptomatic control in acute or sub‑acute disease.
b: Complete removal from the offending environment; provide protective masks if exposure cannot stop.
Bronchodilators only for co‑existent airway obstruction; avoid long‑term high‑dose steroids in chronic fibrosis.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to prevent super‑infection.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of symptoms, lung function, and imaging is essential.
b: Spirometry and DLCO every 3–6 months in chronic disease.
Repeat HRCT if clinical deterioration occurs.
Education on safe handling of agricultural products and use of well‑ventilated storage.

sections.p: Conditions that share cough, dyspnoea, and infiltrates.
b: Sarcoidosis – non‑caseating granulomas, often hilar lymphadenopathy, systemic involvement.
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – usual interstitial pneumonia pattern, no clear exposure.
Asthma – bronchial obstruction, reversible airflow limitation.

sections.p: Certain investigations may be normal early or give false reassurance.
b: Normal chest X‑ray in early acute HP – rely on exposure history.
Negative precipitating antibodies – up to 30 % false‑negative; do not exclude disease.
BAL lymphocytosis may be modest in chronic HP – interpret with clinical context.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness or hypoxia.
Development of chest pain with tachycardia.
Signs of respiratory failure (cyanosis, altered mental status).

faq.q: Why is antigen avoidance more important than steroids?
faq.a: Continued exposure drives ongoing inflammation and fibrosis; steroids only suppress symptoms temporarily.

faq.q: Can HP occur without a known occupational exposure?
faq.a: Yes, domestic exposures (e.g., moldy home‑grown foods) are common in low‑resource settings.

faq.q: Is a normal spirometry enough to rule out HP?
faq.a: No; early disease may have normal lung volumes, so combine with history and imaging.

exam: A farmer presents with fever, cough, and dyspnoea 6 h after cleaning a hay barn. What is the most likely diagnosis and the immediate next step? — Recognise acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis; advise removal from exposure and start short‑course steroids if severe.
How would you differentiate chronic HP from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis on HRCT? — HP shows centrilobular nodules and mosaic attenuation; IPF shows basal honey‑comb without nodules.
A patient with known HP continues to deteriorate despite avoidance. What complication should you screen for? — Pulmonary hypertension; obtain echocardiogram and consider right‑heart catheterisation.
Why are serum precipitating antibodies not definitive for HP? — They may be absent in up to 30 % of cases and can be present in asymptomatic sensitisation.
In a low‑resource clinic without CT, which two investigations are most useful to support HP? — Chest X‑ray for infiltrates and spirometry showing restrictive defect with reduced DLCO.
What are the key elements of patient education to prevent recurrence of HP? — Safe storage of grains, use of protective masks, adequate ventilation, and avoidance of moldy materials.
A patient with sub‑acute HP is started on steroids. What monitoring is required? — Watch for hyperglycaemia, infection, and assess improvement in symptoms and lung function; taper slowly.
Which red‑flag symptom mandates urgent referral to a tertiary centre? — Rapid onset of severe dyspnoea with hypoxia or signs of ARDS.
